intro:
This list is **not meant to be used in full**. Pick **1 resource per skill** (listening, reading, grammar, vocabulary, conversation) and switch when you get tired of it.
• The **top 10** are enough until the end of Genki I.
• The other groups are backups: for when something doesn't work, or when you reach Genki II and beyond.
• Everything here works from English straight into Japanese. The "In Portuguese" group is optional and the course doesn't need it.
• Links checked in September 2026.

groups.title: Start here: your 10 highest-value resources
groups.note: In priority order. Until the end of Genki I, this is enough.

items.name: ToKini Andy – GENKI Grammar Made Clear
items.desc: YouTube playlist in English with one video per Genki I lesson (L1–L12), edited from his live streams and aligned with the 3rd edition; for Genki II (N4, L13–L23) there is a sister playlist, "GENKI 2 Grammar Made Clear", on the same channel.
items.how: After reading the grammar of each Genki lesson, watch the video for the same lesson before doing the workbook; when you reach Genki II, switch to the N4 playlist.

items.name: OTO Navi (official Genki audio)
items.desc: Free official app from The Japan Times (Android and iOS) that plays the textbook and workbook audio (dialogues, vocabulary and listening drills), with repeat and a 3-second skip.
items.how: Every lesson, scan the Genki barcode and listen to the dialogue and vocabulary, repeating each part until you understand all of it.

items.name: GENKI Self-Study Room (official)
items.desc: Free official page for the 3rd edition with dialogue videos, culture-note clips and per-lesson Quizlet sets (vocabulary, conjugation, kanji and kana) for L1–L23.
items.how: During the kana phase, use the kana sets; after that, for each lesson, watch the dialogue video and do that lesson's Quizlet sets.

items.name: Irodori (English edition, Japan Foundation)
items.desc: The Japan Foundation's Irodori course with explanations in English: Starter (A1), Elementary 1 and 2 (A2) and Pre-Intermediate (A2/B1, released 31 Mar 2026), 18 lessons each, as free PDFs with MP3s, word lists and grammar worksheets; free for personal study, with no redistribution or commercial use.
items.how: Every week, do the listening and speaking tasks of the topic that matches your Genki lesson: Starter roughly follows Genki I, Elementary 1–2 roughly follow Genki II, and Pre-Intermediate comes after Genki.

items.name: Anki deck Genki 1 (3rd ed., with audio) → Kaishi 1.5k
items.desc: Free deck with the Genki I vocabulary in per-lesson subdecks and 778 audio files; the next step is Kaishi 1.5k, a deck of 1,501 high-frequency words with audio and pitch (needs Anki 2.1.50+).
items.how: Turn on each lesson's subdeck when you start that Genki lesson, with about 10 min of reviews a day alongside ヅオリンゴー; after Genki I, find Kaishi 1.5k on AnkiWeb and continue with it.

items.name: Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners + Japanese with Shun (Genki podcast)
items.desc: Daily 3–5 minute episodes in slow Japanese (more than 1,590, also on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube); Shun's "Genki Textbook based podcast" on YouTube mainly uses Genki I and II grammar.
items.how: Listen to one Teppei episode a day, replaying the same one several times, and play the Shun episode that matches your Genki lesson during your commute or chores.

items.name: Tadoku – free graded readers
items.desc: Free graded mini-books from NPO Tadoku Supporters, at levels Start and 0 to 5, as printable PDFs; some have narration or a video on YouTube.
items.how: From Genki I lesson 6, read one Level Start or Level 0 book in the Immersion block of your routine, and only move up a level when reading feels comfortable.

items.name: Natural Japanese + にほんごのじかん
items.desc: Comprehensible-input videos filtered by level (formerly Comprehensible Japanese, with more than 1,500 videos, some members-only); Yuki, its best-known teacher, now posts slow, picture-supported videos on the free channel にほんごのじかん.
items.how: During Genki I, watch 20–30 min a day of videos tagged "Complete Beginner", alternating between the two channels.

items.name: OJAD + Kotu (pitch accent)
items.desc: University of Tokyo accent dictionary that shows the pitch of verbs and adjectives in every conjugation, with audio (the interface comes in 15 languages; this link opens the English one); Kotu (kotu.io) is a minimal-pairs perception test.
items.how: When you learn verbs and adjectives in Genki, check their pitch in OJAD and paste the dialogue lines into Suzuki-kun before shadowing; a few times a week, do 5 min of ear training on Kotu.

items.name: EJLX – English-Japanese Language Exchange (Discord)
items.desc: Discord's largest English–Japanese exchange server (85,878 members on 29 Sep 2026), with beginner channels, corrections and voice rooms.
items.how: Post one sentence you wrote yourself each day for correction, using the grammar of your current Genki lesson: it is the most direct practice for learning to build sentences.

groups.title: Genki: official and textbook-aligned material
groups.note: Extras for Genki I and II, for when the top 10 aren't enough.

items.name: Game Gengo – Complete Genki 1: Grammar
items.desc: A second explanation of each Genki I lesson, in English, with examples taken from video games.
items.how: When ToKini Andy's video doesn't click, watch the same lesson here; for Genki II, use the JLPT N4 playlists, because the Genki II playlist has only 2 videos.

items.name: GENKI – sentence-pattern videos (official)
items.desc: Official collection of 132 short skits in Japanese, one for each Genki grammar pattern.
items.how: After studying each grammar point, watch its skit to hear the structure in use, then say a sentence of your own with the same pattern.

items.name: ToKini Andy – The Complete JLPT N5 Kanji Course
items.desc: Playlist of short videos on the stroke order and readings of the N5 kanji.
items.how: From lesson 3, when Genki starts its kanji section (Yomikaki), watch the videos for the lesson's kanji before writing them.

items.name: Anki deck Genki 2 (3rd ed., with audio)
items.desc: Follow-up to the Genki I deck, with the vocabulary of lessons 13 to 23 and 589 audio files.
items.how: When you move to Genki II, repeat the routine: turn on each lesson's subdeck when you start it.

items.name: Anki deck Genki Japanese Vocabulary (sentences + audio + pitch)
items.desc: A fuller alternative to the per-lesson decks, with all the Genki vocabulary in example sentences, 3,080 audio files and a pitch-accent guide; the deck doesn't say which edition it follows.
items.how: Use it instead of the per-lesson decks if you want to see each word inside a sentence, which helps you build your own.

items.name: GENKI Vocab, GENKI Kanji and GENKI Conjugation Cards apps
items.desc: Official paid apps, US$6.99 each on the US App Store; GENKI Kanji covers the book's 317 kanji with stroke-order videos.
items.how: Optional: only buy them if you want everything on your phone, because the free Anki decks and Quizlet sets cover the same content.

items.name: ToKini Andy membership (tokiniandy.com)
items.desc: Optional paid plan (US$10/month or US$120/year, with a free trial mentioned on the site) with Genki 1 and 2 courses, vocabulary decks, kanji and Genki immersion stories.
items.how: Not needed: the free YouTube series is enough; consider it only if you want the extras gathered in one place.

groups.title: In Portuguese (optional)
groups.note: Every resource in this group is in Portuguese (Erin's Challenge is here for its Portuguese subtitles). The course is taught in English and needs none of them; use one only as a fallback when an English explanation doesn't click.

items.name: Irodori in Portuguese (Japan Foundation São Paulo)
items.desc: The Japan Foundation's Irodori course with explanations in Portuguese (Starter A1, with and without romaji, and Elementary 1 and 2, A2), free to download by chapter for personal study, with no redistribution or commercial use; Pre-Intermediate has no Portuguese version yet.
items.how: Not needed: it is the same course as the English edition in "Start here"; open this one only if you want a topic explained in Portuguese.

items.name: Tae Kim – Japanese grammar guide (Portuguese translation)
items.desc: Portuguese translation of Tae Kim's grammar guide, on the official site; it hasn't been confirmed whether it is complete compared with the English original (listed under Grammar).
items.how: Only when a Genki point still isn't clear in English, read the matching section here.

items.name: NHK WORLD-JAPAN – Easy Japanese (Portuguese edition)
items.desc: 48 short audio lessons with PDF text in Portuguese, with free MP3 and PDF downloads; NHK also publishes an English edition of the same course.
items.how: During Genki I, listen to one lesson on your commute and read the PDF afterwards to check what you understood.

items.name: Erin's Challenge! (エリンが挑戦！にほんごできます。)
items.desc: 25 video lessons from the Japan Foundation, in basic and advanced versions, with subtitles in 11 languages including Portuguese (the site interface is in Japanese and English only).
items.how: Watch one skit a week with subtitles, then shadow the key phrases.

items.name: MARUGOTO Japanese Online Course (Japan Foundation, Portuguese page)
items.desc: Structured A1 course with explanations in Portuguese (A2 explanations are only in English, Indonesian and Spanish); it requires registration on JF Minato and has a trial version, and the tutor-supported versions may be paid.
items.how: Use it for review or a change of pace when Genki gets tiring, without switching your main textbook.

items.name: JF Japanese e-Learning Minato
items.desc: Japan Foundation platform, with an interface available in Portuguese, that hosts the JF online courses (kana, kanji, Marugoto and Irodori online); many are free and some are paid.
items.how: During the kana phase, try the kana course; later, use the same account for Marugoto or Irodori online.

items.name: Japan Foundation São Paulo (FJSP)
items.desc: The Japan Foundation's Brazilian centre, in Portuguese, with calls for the free online Marugoto course, Irodori and Erin materials in Portuguese, and events; enrolment dates change.
items.how: Check the site once a quarter so you don't miss open enrolments.

items.name: Programa Japonês Online (YouTube)
items.desc: Channel with short beginner lessons in which the Portuguese videos are the older ones (recent ones have English titles); its paid school is at programajaponesonline.com.br.
items.how: Search the channel for the Genki point you're studying to hear it explained in Portuguese.

items.name: VideoAulas de Japonês – Absolute Beginner course
items.desc: 26-lesson course for absolute beginners, in Portuguese; the channel hasn't posted in about 2 years, but the lessons are still online.
items.how: In the first weeks, use it alongside Genki lessons 1 to 3 as an extra explanation in Portuguese.

items.name: Kultivi – Basic Japanese course
items.desc: Free video course in Portuguese on the writing systems and the basics, with about 30 hours of content and exercises according to search results (not reviewed in depth).
items.how: Use it in the first month, during the kana phase, as a backup explanation in Portuguese.

items.name: JapaLab (Hiru Miyamoto)
items.desc: N4 and N3 grammar series explained in Portuguese by a Brazilian who has lived in Japan for more than 25 years; the video titles are in English.
items.how: Save it for Genki II onwards, when you want to review N4 or N3 grammar in Portuguese.

items.name: Kotobá Japonês Fluente (podcast)
items.desc: Bilingual Japanese–Portuguese conversation episodes that end with a key-vocabulary recap; it is a school, so it also sells paid courses.
items.how: From Genki II, listen to one episode a week and add the recap words to ヅオリンゴー.

items.name: HAJIMARU – Japan Foundation São Paulo podcast
items.desc: Monthly talks in Portuguese on Japanese language, culture and research, since March 2025; the latest episode seen is from 26 Jun 2026, so it may be on a break.
items.how: Listen for motivation and cultural context, not as Japanese listening practice.

items.name: Japonês Brasil (Discord)
items.desc: Brazilian community, in Portuguese, for sharing materials and JLPT and scholarship information, with about 2.6K members on its DISBOARD listing on 29 Sep 2026.
items.how: Join through the DISBOARD button to ask questions in Portuguese and follow JLPT and scholarship notices.

groups.title: Listening: comprehensible input and podcasts
groups.note: From easiest to hardest. One channel at a time is enough.

items.name: Japanese with Shun (main channel)
items.desc: Easy vlogs and N5–N4 podcast episodes in clear Japanese, with the playlists "Japanese with Shun (Podcast)" and "Oyasumi Japanese with Shun".
items.how: When the Genki-based podcast gets easy, move on to the channel's vlogs and podcasts in the Immersion block.

items.name: IRODORI Japanese Online Course
items.desc: Interactive online version of Irodori (Starter and Elementary 1–2) on the JF Minato platform, with explanations in 8 or more languages.
items.how: On days away from the textbook, do the listening and speaking tasks of your current Irodori topic here.

items.name: MARUGOTO Plus
items.desc: Free Japan Foundation site with conversation videos and culture content at A1 and A2, plus the MARUGOTO-NO-KOTOBA vocabulary.
items.how: Watch one conversation video per Genki lesson as extra listening.

items.name: Learn Japanese Pod (Alex & Ami)
items.desc: Conversation podcast for absolute beginners explained in English, so it has no immersion value, and with little activity (last video about 8 months ago).
items.how: Save it for low-energy days, as light listening.

items.name: Miku Real Japanese
items.desc: Active channel in Japanese with the playlist "Grammar videos【N5/N4】" (95 videos) and N3/N2 listening and conversation videos; some podcasts are members-only.
items.how: During Genki, use the N5/N4 grammar playlist to review the lesson's points and leave the N3/N2 videos for later.

items.name: Speak Japanese Naturally
items.desc: Walk-and-talk scenery videos in simple Japanese, some with a PDF, on a channel that says it is made for beginners.
items.how: From late N4, use it as relaxed listening in the Immersion block.

items.name: Nihongo con Teppei (main series) and Teppei Z
items.desc: Teppei's main series, at lower-intermediate level, which Teppei Z continues at the same level.
items.how: Move here when you reach N3 and the beginner series feels easy.

items.name: EASY JAPANESE PODCAST (Masa & Asami)
items.desc: Conversation podcast about everyday life, mostly at N3 level according to the channel itself, with more than 945 episodes and subtitled versions.
items.how: At N3, listen to the subtitled version of an episode first, then to the version without subtitles.

items.name: YUYUの日本語Podcast
items.desc: Natural-speed conversations, in Japanese only, about culture and learning; not for beginners.
items.how: Keep it for the N3 to N1 stage, when you want to stretch your listening.

groups.title: Reading: graded readers and easy news
groups.note: From easiest to hardest. Tadoku is already in "Start here".

items.name: Hirogaru (ひろがる)
items.desc: Hobby-themed articles and videos (food, sports, anime and more) at A1–A2 level, with difficult-word lists on the English page; the site's security certificate failed one automated check.
items.how: After Genki I, read an article on a topic you like when you need motivation.

items.name: NHK NEWS WEB EASY
items.desc: Simplified news with furigana and audio; on your first visit, the site asks you to accept its terms and choose a usage purpose.
items.how: From late N4, read one article a day with Yomitan installed.

items.name: 福娘童話集 (folktales)
items.desc: About 3,200 short tales, many with audio narration and some with English translations, on an ad-supported site.
items.how: From N4, read and listen to one tale before bed.

items.name: YomuJP (Kurosio)
items.desc: Level-tagged articles from N6 (below N5) to N1, with no audio; new articles are free for 4 weeks and then subscribers-only.
items.how: From N4 on, use it as your main reading ladder, moving up a level when it feels comfortable.

items.name: Todaii Japanese
items.desc: Graded news app (formerly easyjapanese.net) with furigana, audio and a built-in dictionary, for iOS and Android, with a premium plan.
items.how: Use it on your phone as an alternative to NHK Easy when you're away from the computer.

items.name: Satori Reader
items.desc: Serialized stories with audio, tap-to-define and explanation notes; some episodes are free and the Pro plan costs US$9/month or US$89/year.
items.how: After Genki II, try the free episodes before thinking about subscribing.

items.name: Aozora Bunko (青空文庫)
items.desc: Library of literary works, mostly public domain in Japan, in which classic prose uses older spelling and vocabulary.
items.how: At N2–N1, start with short stories from the modern era.

groups.title: Grammar: explanations and lists
groups.note: A second explanation and milestone review. ToKini Andy is already in "Start here".

items.name: Japanese Ammo with Misa – grammar for absolute beginners
items.desc: Very thorough lessons, in English, on particles and basic sentence structure.
items.how: Whenever you get stuck on は/が/に/で while building sentences in Genki I, watch the lesson on that particle and write three sentences of your own with it.

items.name: Tae Kim's Guide to Learning Japanese
items.desc: Free written grammar guide, also available as a PDF, whose server is sometimes down and whose license (CC BY-NC-SA) forbids any commercial use.
items.how: Look up the section for the Genki point you're studying when you want a written explanation.

items.name: JLPT Sensei – N5–N1 grammar lists
items.desc: Unofficial grammar lists by level, with examples for each point, on an ad-supported site (change "n5" in the URL to the level you want).
items.how: Use it for a quick look-up of a point and as a checklist as you approach each JLPT milestone.

items.name: tanos.co.uk – JLPT N5–N1 lists
items.desc: Open (CC BY) vocabulary, kanji and grammar lists by level, with .doc, .pdf and .anki downloads; they are estimates based on the pre-2010 lists, and the site hasn't been updated since November 2010.
items.how: Before closing a milestone, check that level's list for items you haven't covered yet.

items.name: Game Gengo – JLPT N5 Grammar
items.desc: Playlist with all the N5 grammar, from a channel that also has N4, N3 and N2+ versions and an N5 vocabulary series.
items.how: Near the end of Genki I, review the whole playlist before the N5 milestone.

items.name: Japanese Ammo with Misa – upper beginner and lower intermediate
items.desc: Grammar lessons for learners past the basics, from a channel that also has a JLPT N3 course playlist.
items.how: During Genki II, use it as a second explanation of the lesson's points.

items.name: Kaname Naito
items.desc: Videos in English on the nuances of word usage, grammar and dialogues, with playlists for grammar, "Word Usage", "Pronunciation" and "Dialogues".
items.how: From Genki II, watch one video a week, especially when two similar expressions get mixed up.

items.name: Bunpro (grammar SRS)
items.desc: Grammar SRS whose free plan only shows the grammar pages and readings; premium costs US$5/month or US$150 lifetime, with a 30-day trial that needs no card.
items.how: Optional from Genki II, if you want spaced-repetition grammar review on top of ヅオリンゴー.

items.name: Game Gengo – JLPT N4 Grammar
items.desc: N4 grammar review in 5 long videos.
items.how: Watch it after Genki II, as review for the N4 milestone.

items.name: 日本語の森 (Nihongo no Mori)
items.desc: JLPT-oriented lessons, almost all in Japanese, on the @nihongonomori2013 channel (not @nihongonomori).
items.how: Use it as your main video source when preparing for the N3 to N1 milestones.

items.name: Game Gengo – JLPT N2 Grammar
items.desc: N2 grammar review, from a channel that also has the "Complete N2 Grammar" playlist.
items.how: Watch it alongside Sou Matome or Shin Kanzen Master N2.

items.name: Game Gengo – JLPT N1 Grammar
items.desc: Overview of N1 grammar in 3 long videos.
items.how: Watch it before the final milestone, N1.

items.name: IMABI
items.desc: In-depth, dense grammar reference, from beginner to classical Japanese, currently being remodelled.
items.how: Not for your first pass: from N3, look things up here when you need the nuance of a point.

groups.title: Vocabulary and kanji: SRS and dictionaries
groups.note: Your main SRS is ヅオリンゴー; these only come in when something is missing.

items.name: Jisho.org
items.desc: Online dictionary of words, kanji and example sentences.
items.how: Use it as your everyday dictionary whenever a new word shows up in Genki or Wagotabi.

items.name: Tatoeba
items.desc: Collaborative database of example sentences with translations, of variable quality (prefer sentences from native speakers).
items.how: When you build a sentence with a new word, search for examples of it here and reuse the structure, swapping in your own words.

items.name: Kanji alive
items.desc: Openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) kanji data with stroke-order animations and audio examples, plus a web app.
items.how: When you learn each Genki lesson's kanji, watch the stroke animation and listen to the examples.

items.name: Anki
items.desc: Spaced-repetition app that runs every deck on this list, syncing through a free AnkiWeb account; it is free on desktop and Android (AnkiDroid), and AnkiMobile for iOS costs US$24.99.
items.how: Install it to use the Genki decks and Kaishi; the rest of your vocabulary can stay in ヅオリンゴー.

items.name: renshuu
items.desc: Gamified vocabulary, kanji and grammar drills with ready-made packs for each Genki lesson, all free and without limits; Pro only adds conveniences.
items.how: If you prefer gamification to Anki, turn on the pack for your current Genki lesson.

items.name: JLPT Tango N5 (Anki)
items.desc: Sentence-based deck with 1,186 notes and audio, copied from the book "JLPT Tango" (a legal grey area); the same author has an N4 version.
items.how: Optional: use it only to fill gaps before the N5 milestone, and prefer Kaishi or the Genki decks.

items.name: Yomitan
items.desc: Pop-up dictionary browser extension: hover over Japanese text to see the definition and create Anki cards with one click.
items.how: Install it when you reach N4 to read NHK Easy, Satori and Japanese websites.

items.name: Core 2k/6k Optimized (Anki)
items.desc: Classic frequency deck, with 2,000 notes and audio in part 1 (updated in 2017) and parts 2 and 3 going up to 6,000 words.
items.how: After Genki, choose either this or Kaishi 1.5k to expand your vocabulary, never both.

items.name: jpdb.io
items.desc: Free site with more than 21,000 frequency-sorted vocabulary decks for specific anime, novels and visual novels, plus a text reader; the optional Patreon only adds small extras.
items.how: From N4, study the deck for an anime or book before watching or reading it.

items.name: Ankidrone Essentials
items.desc: Deck of about 8,000 cards covering JLPT Tango N5 to N1, built from the copyrighted books (the same legal grey area), with the download hosted off-site.
items.how: From N3 on, consider it as a single long-term vocabulary deck.

items.name: WaniKani
items.desc: Kanji and vocabulary SRS (about 2,000 kanji and 6,000 words) with levels 1 to 3 free and then US$9/month, US$89/year or US$299 lifetime, in a kanji order different from Genki's.
items.how: Optional: try the free levels only if Genki's kanji pace feels too slow.

groups.title: Pronunciation and pitch accent
groups.note: OJAD and Kotu are already in "Start here".

items.name: Wiktionary – Tokyo pitch accent
items.desc: English entries that give the Tokyo accent type with IPA (for example, 東京 = heiban [0]), with uneven coverage for rarer words.
items.how: Look a word up here when it isn't in OJAD.

items.name: WasedaX – Japanese Pronunciation for Communication (edX)
items.desc: 5-week beginner course on accent and intonation, taught in Japanese, with free audit access and a paid US$129 certificate.
items.how: Near the end of Genki I, take the course as an auditor (free).

items.name: Dogen – Japanese Phonetics (Patreon)
items.desc: Systematic pitch-accent course on Patreon (a US$15 tier for the Japanese Phonetics series and group lessons), with a free YouTube channel.
items.how: Optional: only subscribe once you decide to take pronunciation seriously; until then, use the free channel for motivation.

groups.title: Conversation and getting corrected
groups.note: Writing sentences and getting them corrected is what best tackles your biggest difficulty. EJLX is already in "Start here".

items.name: HelloTalk
items.desc: Exchange app where natives correct your posts ("moments") and you swap text and voice messages with Japanese people learning English or Portuguese; it has a paid VIP plan.
items.how: Write one short post a day with the grammar of your current Genki lesson and let natives correct it.

items.name: italki (paid tutors)
items.desc: Private lessons paid per lesson, with no subscription, costing about US$4–40 for Japanese (US$4–20 with community tutors) according to italki's 2026 blog, with trial lessons 30–50% cheaper.
items.how: From mid-Genki I on, take one or two 30-min lessons a week to rehearse the lesson's dialogue and can-dos.

items.name: Tandem
items.desc: Language-exchange app for finding conversation partners, free to download, with a Pro plan.
items.how: Save it for late Genki II, when you can already hold a basic conversation.

items.name: VRC EN-JP Language Exchange (VRChat)
items.desc: VRChat group, with its own Discord, that holds live meetups with Japanese natives in a VR headset or desktop mode; the schedule was not re-checked.
items.how: Once you can hold a basic conversation, join a meetup to speak without pressure.

groups.title: After Genki: textbooks and next steps
groups.note: Suggested order: Quartet I → II or Tobira; then Sou Matome → Shin Kanzen Master for the JLPT milestones. TRY! bridges textbook style and exam style.

items.name: QUARTET I and II (Japan Times)
items.desc: Intermediate textbooks from the same publisher and in the same style as Genki (2 textbooks and 2 workbooks), aimed at learners with about 250–300 hours of study, with free answer keys, can-do lists and author videos on the site, and audio on OTO Navi.
items.how: First choice after Genki II: do Quartet I, then Quartet II.

items.name: ToKini Andy – Quartet 1
items.desc: Playlist with lesson-by-lesson videos for Quartet I, which the channel labels N3.
items.how: If you choose Quartet, watch each lesson's video after studying it, as you did with Genki.

items.name: ToKini Andy – Quartet 2
items.desc: Companion playlist for Quartet II (N2), from a channel that also has Quartet practice and live-stream playlists.
items.how: Follow the same routine when you move on to Quartet II.

items.name: Tobira: Gateway to Advanced Japanese (Kurosio)
items.desc: Paid textbook, an alternative to Quartet, whose site offers free audio, kanji, vocabulary and grammar materials and videos.
items.how: After Genki II, choose either this or Quartet, not both.

items.name: Tobira Study Resources
items.desc: Free vocabulary, grammar and kanji exercises for all 15 Tobira lessons, based on the book.
items.how: If you choose Tobira, do each lesson's exercises after studying it.

items.name: 日本語総まとめ (Sou Matome) – ASK
items.desc: Light review books, one page a day for 6–8 weeks, split by skill from N3 to N1 (33 titles in total).
items.how: Use them as the first prep pass for each JLPT milestone from N3 on.

items.name: 新完全マスター (Shin Kanzen Master) – 3A
items.desc: Demanding JLPT drill books, one per skill (grammar, reading, listening, vocabulary and kanji); the N3 grammar book costs ¥1,320 including tax.
items.how: Use them as a second pass, after Sou Matome, before the N3, N2 and N1 milestones.

items.name: TRY! 日本語能力試験 (ASK)
items.desc: Grammar-first JLPT books with conversation and reading contexts, at levels START and N5–N1, with an e-learning version (eTRY!).
items.how: At N3 and N2, use them as a bridge between textbook style and exam style.

groups.title: Use with caution: discontinued or inactive
groups.note: Still online, but they stopped or lost content. Don't build your study around them.

items.name: Genki Study Resources (emptied)
items.desc: Genki exercise site that had all its exercises removed at The Japan Times' request; only the help pages, such as the Anki deck list, still work.
items.how: Don't rely on it: use only the Anki deck page and avoid copies that re-host the exercises.

items.name: Watanoc (inactive since 2016)
items.desc: Easy-Japanese web magazine with short articles tagged N5 to N3; there have been no new posts since October 2016, but the archive is still online.
items.how: Use it only now and then, as light extra reading.

items.name: Onomappu (archive)
items.desc: Channel about onomatopoeia and daily life that stopped posting (the last video is called "My Last YouTube Video"), but keeps its archive online.
items.how: At N4–N3, watch it for fun to learn onomatopoeia.

items.name: Cure Dolly – Japanese from scratch (archive)
items.desc: Course of about 93 videos with an alternative view of particles and sentence structure that deliberately contradicts textbook terminology; the creator died in 2021, but the videos are still online.
items.how: Use it only as a second perspective when sentence structure doesn't make sense, never as your main path.
